newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Treasury projects NZ growth rate peak of 4.2 pct.
newsitem.headline: Treasury projects NZ growth rate peak of 4.2 pct.

text.p: The Treasury in budget documents on Thursday projected New Zealand's economic growth rate would peak at 4.2 percent in the year to March 1999.

On an annual average basis, it forecast growth would ease from 3.1 percent in 1996 to 2.5 percent in 1997 and 2.4 percent in 1998, before rising to 4.2 percent in 1999 and then slipping back to 3.5 percent in 2000.

Slower than previously forecast growth in the early part of the cycle would reduce inflationary pressures in the short-term but monetary conditions would need to tighten from early 1998, Treasury said in its Economic and Fiscal Update.
The Statistics Department said in its latest figures that the economy grew a seasonally adjusted 2.9 percent in the 1996 year.

Treasury's forecasts compare with the independent Institute of Economic Research forecast of growth rising from 2.1 percent in the year to March 1997, to 2.5 percent in 1998 and peaking at 4.3 percent in 1999.
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand, due to publish new forecasts on Friday, in March forecast growth of 2.0 in 1997, 2.7 percent in 1998, 3.9 percent in 1999 and 2.8 percent in 2000.
Treasury said an upturn in growth is anticipated towards the end of 1997 with past falls in interest rates boosting spending.
"With confidence improving, a cycle of increased demand and production would be set in motion," it said.
Momentum would increase in 1998/99 as increased government spending, tax reduction, the lagged effects of an earlier monetary easing and strong world growth took effect.
Treasurer Winston Peters told journalists he did not think Treasury's forecasts were overly optimistic.
"I think if anything we have erred on the conservative side," he said.
"We are very confident of the economy growing."
He said tariff reform, electricity industry reform and an attack on compliance costs would underpin accelerating growth.
"The envirnoment for business to thrive is there," Peters said.
He said if a referendum on compulsory pensions in September is accepted it would only have a limited effect on the growth rate.
Treasury forecasts underlying inflation would fall to 1.0 percent in the year to March 1998 from 2.0 percent in March 1997 and then rise to 1.3 percent in 1999 and 1.6 percent in 2000.
It expects 90-day bank bills to average 7.6 percent in 1997/98 against just under 7.0 percent at present, and rise to an average of 8.6 percent in 1998/99 before easing to 7.4 percent in 2000.
The New Zealand dollar Trade-Weighted Index is forecast to stay between 68.0 and 69.5 on average from 1997/98 through to 1999/2000.
The current account deficit is forecast to peak at $5.7 billion, 5.5 percent of GDP, in 1999/2000.
Unemployment is forecast to rise to 6.8 percent in 1998 from 6.4 percent in 1997 before falling down to 5.7 percent in 2000.
